# Report on `region.fasta` (`region_007`)

## Summary
The 3,000-bp region is a bacterial-style sequence (51.0% G+C, no ambiguous bases, no long homopolymers or obvious low-complexity/tandem-repeat tracts). **It contains one dominant, unambiguous protein-coding gene that is far longer and more hydrophobic than chance would produce — apparently a polytopic integral membrane protein (transporter/permease-like).** Nothing else in the sequence is strongly diagnostic.

## 1. A long, highly hydrophobic open reading frame (the main finding)
| Feature | Coordinate (1-based) |
|---|---|
| ORF start (ATG) | **1085–1087** |
| Coding sequence | **1085–2623** |
| Stop codon (TGA) | **2624–2626** |
| Total ORF (incl. stop) | **1085–2626**, 1,542 bp |
| Encoded protein | **513 aa**, strand **+** |

This ORF is ~2.3× larger than the largest ORF found in 300 length-matched random sequences (median 288 bp, max 684 bp), so it is not a chance product.

**Protein properties.** The 513-aa product is strongly hydrophobic (66.5% of residues in the hydrophobic set A,V,I,L,M,F,W,Y,P,G), with especially high Leu (83) and Ile/Ala/Val content — the classic signature of a membrane protein. Kyte–Doolittle hydropathy analysis predicts roughly **9–12 transmembrane α-helices**, heavily clustered in the N-terminal half:

| Predicted TM helix (approx.) | Residues | Nucleotide span |
|---|---|---|
| TM1 | 22–43 | 1148–1214 |
| TM2 | 40–61 | 1202–1268 |
| TM3 | 95–116 | 1367–1433 |
| TM4 | 111–132 | 1415–1481 |
| TM5 | 134–155 | 1484–1550 |
| TM6 | 239–260 | 1799–1865 |
| TM7 | 309–330 | 2009–2075 |
| TM8 | 347–368 | 2123–2189 |
| TM9 | 474–495 | 2504–2570 |

(The N-terminal region aa ~19–170 behaves as one extended hydrophobic block; depending on the threshold it resolves into 4–6 closely spaced helices.) The overall architecture — a hydrophobic N-terminal helix bundle with a more polar C-terminal half — is typical of secondary transporters/permeases. Sequence inspection alone cannot assign a specific family.

## 2. Flanking signals
- **Ribosome-binding-site-like sequence upstream of the ORF:** a purine-rich stretch at roughly **1055–1080** (…AAGGTAAGGGAAACCATC-ATG), ~5–30 nt 5′ of the start codon.
- **Stem–loop (possible rho-independent terminator) immediately downstream of the ORF:** at **2636–2657** there is a perfect 8-bp GC-rich inverted repeat (5′-ACCGGGCA … TGCCCGGT) with the loop TATAAA, followed by a T-rich tract (2658–2670) — consistent with a transcription terminator just past the gene end.
- **A second hairpin** at approximately **104–125** (GC-rich inverted repeat with a T-rich 3′ tail) occurs in the 5′ portion of the region, where it could act as a regulatory terminator/attenuator.

## 3. Other (minor) ORFs
A few shorter ORFs exist but none has the coding hallmarks of the big one:
- **214–627** (+ strand), 137 aa — a fairly polar/charged peptide; plausibly a real but short gene or part of a 5′ gene.
- **677–880** (+ strand), 67 aa.
- **2137–2856** (− strand), 239 aa — an antisense ORF that overlaps the main gene; it encodes a more soluble-looking protein. Because antisense overlap of this kind is uncommon and short ORFs on the opposite strand arise readily by chance, this should be treated cautiously unless corroborated.

## Bottom line
The region harbors a single clear gene at **nt 1085–2626** encoding a **513-residue, ~9–12-transmembrane-segment integral membrane protein**, with a plausible RBS upstream and a likely rho-independent terminator downstream. This is the notable feature; the remainder of the sequence contains only short/spurious ORFs and two short hairpins and does not show other striking anomalies.
